O R I E N TAT I O N
How to use this coursebook
Year 3 is where several familiar ideas become tools for general reasoning.
A letter starts to stand for a family of numbers, a table of values becomes a
relationship, a drawing becomes evidence for a claim, and a set of
measurements becomes an argument about uncertainty.
You already know how to calculate with whole
numbers, fractions and decimals. You have
met negative numbers, simple equations and
the basic properties of shapes. This course
asks you to work with those ideas at a different
level: to explain why a rule always works, to
choose an efficient representation, to connect
an equation with its graph, and to decide when
a numerical answer is precise enough to be
useful.
The book is arranged in four parts. Part I
builds the number system and algebraic
structure that the rest of the course depends
on: irrational numbers, exponent laws,
scientific notation, functions and algebraic
manipulation. Part II turns that structure into
relationships: gradient and intercept, linear
models, equations, inequalities and systems.
Part III is geometry as a deductive discipline:
transformations, congruence, similarity, right-
triangle trigonometry, and the measurement
of solids. Part IV examines data and chance,
with particular attention to the difference
between a pattern in data and a causal claim.
Every chapter follows the same inquiry
rhythm. A situation raises a question;
definitions and representations give you the
tools to investigate it; worked examples make
the reasoning visible; graded practice makes
the method dependable; an investigation, an
application and a criterion task ask you to use
the mathematics beyond the original example.
The answer section confirms your reasoning
rather than replacing it.

H OW T H E L A B E L S WO R K
Definition boxes state precise meanings. Key idea boxes connect a method to a larger
principle. Strategy boxes give a reusable procedure. Common error boxes show a mistake
worth anticipating. ATL boxes make a learning skill explicit and give you a way to practise it.
Criterion strips name the MYP criterion and strands developed by a section.
AT L · U S I N G T H E A N S W E R K E Y W E L L
Attempt the question fully before
checking. If your answer differs, locate
the first line where your reasoning
diverges. Mark the correction in a
different colour and write one sentence
explaining why the alternative was
wrong. That sentence is often more
valuable than the correct number.
ACA D E M I C H O N E S T Y
Copying a solution without
understanding it creates the appearance
of progress and hides a gap. Use sample
answers to compare methods, not to
replace your attempt. In investigations,
report your own data and reasoning, and
acknowledge any source you use.

T H E P R O G R A M M E I N P R A C T I C E
The MYP framework in this course
The Middle Years Programme asks students to learn mathematics as a
connected, conceptual and applicable discipline. Concepts organise the
content, contexts give it purpose, and criteria make the quality of thinking
visible.
Aims of MYP mathematics
The MYP mathematics framework aims to help students enjoy mathematics, develop curiosity and
confidence, build conceptual understanding, apply mathematics to authentic situations,
communicate reasoning, think critically and creatively, and appreciate the international and
historical dimensions of the subject. In Year 3, the emphasis shifts from describing procedures to
explaining structure: why exponent laws follow from repeated multiplication, why a linear
function has constant gradient, why congruence can be established from limited information, and
why correlation alone cannot establish causation.
K E Y C O N C E P T 0 1
Form
The shape, structure and
organisation of
mathematical objects:
the form of a prime
factorisation, the form of
a linear equation, the
form of a geometrical
proof. Form helps us
notice what is
mathematically the same
beneath different
appearances.
K E Y C O N C E P T 0 2
Logic
The reasoning that
connects claims to
conclusions. Logic asks
not only “Is it true?” but
“How do we know, and
for which cases?” It is the
discipline behind
classification, deduction,
counterexample and
generalisation.
K E Y C O N C E P T 0 3
Relationships
Connections between
quantities, variables,
representations and
ideas. A function, a
graph, a ratio, a
similarity statement and
a trend line are different
ways of expressing
relationships.
Related concepts used in this course
CHANGE
How one quantity responds when
another changes.
EQUIVALENCE
Different forms with the same
value or meaning.
GENERALISATION
Extending a relationship to a
whole class of cases.
JUSTIFICATION
Reasons and evidence that
support a claim.
MEASUREMENT
Assigning numbers and units to
attributes of objects.
MODELS
Simplified representations of a
real situation.
PATTERNS
Regular structure that repeats or
grows predictably.
QUANTITY
Number, magnitude, measure and
unit.
REPRESENTATION
Words, symbols, tables, diagrams
and graphs.

Global contexts
Each chapter is anchored in one of the six MYP global contexts. The context is not decoration: it
shapes the questions asked, the data used and the kind of solution that counts as useful.
GLOBAL CONTEXT
HOW MATHEMATICS ENTERS THE INQUIRY
Identities and relationships
How categories, groups and belonging can be described and interrogated;
how similarity and scale connect objects while preserving identity of
shape.
Orientation in space and
time
How number systems, calendars and measurement developed across
cultures; how coordinates, transformations and scale structure space.
Personal and cultural
expression
How proportion, pattern and geometry shape music, design, craft and
architecture; how tessellation and symmetry create visual order.
Scientific and technical
innovation
How accurate measurement, formulas, scientific notation and data
displays support invention, engineering and scientific claims.
Fairness and development
How budgets, percentages, comparisons and data can support or distort
fair decisions; how samples and claims can mislead.
Globalization and
sustainability
How quantities are compared across communities and environments, and
how claims about resources and risk are communicated.
Inquiry in a mathematics lesson
Inquiry does not mean that students are left to rediscover every definition without guidance. It
means that a question genuinely drives the sequence of work, that students make and test
conjectures, and that they can explain how a result was reached. The course uses a repeating
pathway.

pattern or claim
that is not yet
explainable.

against further

5

evidence and the

Approaches to learning
ATL skills are not an extra syllabus. They are the practices that make mathematical learning
transferable. Each chapter names one ATL focus and gives a concrete way to practise it.

A S S E S S M E N T F O R U N D E R S TA N D I N G
Assessment criteria in practice
MYP mathematics uses four criteria. They describe different qualities of
mathematical work, not four separate syllabuses. A single rich task can
provide evidence for more than one criterion.
How the criteria work together
A criterion task in this book names the criteria it is designed to evidence. A task may, for example,
ask you to model a situation (A), identify and generalise a pattern (B), present the reasoning (C) and
evaluate the accuracy and meaning of the result (D). Not every exercise needs all four criteria.
Short fluency exercises usually provide evidence for A only; an investigation may provide evidence
for B and C; a modelling task may provide evidence for A, C and D.
A
KNOWING AND UNDERSTANDING
Select appropriate mathematics for
familiar and unfamiliar problems.
Apply the selected mathematics
successfully.
Solve problems correctly across a range of
contexts.
In this course: number systems, exponent
laws, function notation, linear equations,
angle and circle facts, trigonometry,
surface area and volume.
B
INVESTIGATING PATTERNS
Apply problem-solving techniques to
recognise patterns.
Describe patterns as relationships or
general rules consistent with findings.
Verify whether a pattern works for other
examples.
In this course: growth patterns, gradient
and rate of change, transformation
mappings, similarity ratios, scaling of
volume, trends in bivariate data.
C
COMMUNICATING
Use appropriate mathematical language,
notation and symbols.
Use different forms of representation and
move between them.
Present complete, coherent and concise
lines of reasoning.
Organise information using a logical
structure.
In this course: function notation, set and
interval notation, congruence statements,
two-column and paragraph proofs,
labelled graphs and units.
D
APPLYING MATHEMATICS IN REAL-LIFE
CONTEXTS
Identify relevant elements of authentic
situations.
Select and apply mathematical strategies.
Justify the degree of accuracy of a
solution.
Justify whether the solution makes sense
in context.
In this course: data plans, ramp design,
packaging, urban planning, survey
sampling, risk communication and
evidence evaluation.

WHAT TO SHOW
WHAT STRONG WORK LOOKS LIKE
Selection
The chosen method fits the structure of the problem, and an alternative
was considered where relevant.
Application
Each step is mathematically valid, notation is accurate, and the result is
checked against the context.
Justification
Claims are supported by reasons, definitions or evidence; a generalisation
is distinguished from a set of examples.
Communication
A reader can follow the reasoning without reconstructing missing steps;
diagrams and units are purposeful.
Evaluation
Limitations, assumptions and the appropriateness of the accuracy are
stated, not merely implied.
Formative practice is not a formal assessment
Most questions in this book are practice, not summative assessment. Their purpose is to produce
feedback: an error is information about what to practise next. Criterion tasks at the end of each
chapter are longer and are accompanied by a planning frame and a course rubric. Teachers should
apply their school’s official assessment descriptors and procedures; the bands in this book are
teaching summaries, not official IB level descriptors.
A N OT E O N C O M M A N D T E R M S
State requires a short answer without justification. Describe requires relevant features.
Explain requires reasons or mechanisms. Justify requires evidence or a valid argument.
Evaluate requires a judgment supported by criteria. Investigate requires a planned process,
data or examples, a pattern, and a conclusion. The command term tells you how much
reasoning to show, not how long the answer must be.

How the parts build on one another
Part I
Structure before method
Irrational numbers extend the number line;
exponent laws compress repeated
multiplication; algebraic notation names a
function. Without this structure, later
procedures are memorised rather than
understood.
Part II
Relationships as objects
Linear functions connect tables, graphs,
equations and contexts. Solving equations and
systems is then a question about intersection
and balance, not a sequence of arbitrary
moves.
Part III
Reasoning about space
Transformations make congruence precise.
Similarity makes trigonometric ratios possible.
Solids turn those ratios into volume and
surface area, including the surprising cube law
for scaling.
Part IV
Evidence and uncertainty
Bivariate data connects algebra and statistics.
Probability quantifies uncertainty. Sampling
explains why a claim from data needs a
method, a margin of doubt and a causal
argument.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Form. A number has more than one possible
written form: fraction, terminating decimal,
repeating decimal, surd or approximation. The
form reveals which operations are exact and
which are limited.
Quantity. The real number line assigns a position
to every decimal, including those with infinitely
many digits. Order and distance can be described
without listing every digit.
Equivalence. Different decimals, fractions and
radical expressions can name the same real
number. Recognising equivalence is central to
simplifying and to proving.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Orientation in space and time. Exploration:
how different cultures represented and
approximated quantities, and why the
discovery of incommensurable lengths
challenged the idea that all lengths could be
expressed as whole-number ratios.
Greek mathematicians initially assumed
that any two lengths could be compared
using a common unit. The diagonal of a
square exposed a length with no such
common unit. That discovery did not break
mathematics; it forced a broader
conception of number. Today, irrational
numbers appear in geometry, music theory,
engineering tolerances and computer
graphics.

TERMINATING AND REPEATING DECIMALS
A rational number is a quotient of two integers. That simple definition unifies whole
numbers, fractions, terminating decimals and repeating decimals: they are different
surface forms of the same underlying structure.
Every integer is rational: 
 and 
. Every terminating decimal is rational because it can
be written over a power of 10: 
. A repeating decimal is also rational, although that is
less obvious. The repetition is the clue: it allows a finite algebraic calculation to recover an exact
fraction.
Not all rational numbers have terminating decimals. In lowest terms, the denominator decides. If
the denominator has only prime factors 2 and 5, the decimal terminates, because multiplying
numerator and denominator by a suitable power of 10 produces an equivalent fraction with
denominator 
. If the denominator has any other prime factor, the decimal repeats forever.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Patterns. The exponent laws are not arbitrary
rules; they record what happens when we count
repeated factors. The pattern continues
consistently from positive to zero to negative
exponents.
Quantity. Scientific notation separates the size of
a quantity (the power of 10) from its significant
digits (the mantissa), making comparisons of
scale immediate.
Representation. A number can be written in
standard form, factor form, index form or
scientific notation. Each representation
highlights a different property.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Scientific and technical innovation.
Exploration: how scientists and engineers
communicate measurements across
radically different scales, from the diameter
of an atom to the distance between galaxies,
and why a shared notation is essential for
collaboration.
Scientific notation is a technology of
communication as much as a mathematical
convenience. It makes the order of
magnitude visible, supports reliable
calculation with calculators and computers,
and forces the writer to state how many
digits are actually meaningful.

Scientific notation writes a number as a mantissa between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power
of 10. The power of 10 carries the order of magnitude; the mantissa carries the meaningful
digits.
To convert

. The
point moved four places, so 
. To convert

to get 7.2; moving right corresponds to a negative exponent, so 
. The number of
places moved is always the absolute value of the exponent.

Scale is approximate; each marker names an order of magnitude, not an exact measurement.
Figure 2.3 Each step of one on the scale represents a factor of 10. Scientific notation compresses this vast range into a mantissa
and an exponent.
Multiplication and division use the exponent laws directly. Multiply the mantissas, then add the
exponents; divide the mantissas, then subtract the exponents. If the resulting mantissa is not
between 1 and 10, adjust it by moving the decimal point and changing the exponent. Addition and
subtraction require a common exponent before the mantissas can be combined.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Relationships. A linear relationship connects
two quantities by a constant rate of change. The
same relationship can be represented by a table,
a graph, an equation or a description in words.
Change. Gradient measures how quickly the
dependent quantity changes as the independent
quantity increases by one unit. A zero gradient
and an undefined gradient describe very
different situations.
Representation. Each representation exposes
different information. A table shows individual
values, a graph shows shape and direction, and
an equation gives the exact rule.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Fairness and development. Exploration:
how linear cost models can make charges
predictable, and how a fixed fee, a rate or a
cap affects different users unequally.
Two businesses may describe their prices
with straight lines that look equally simple.
The intercept says how much someone pays
before using anything; the gradient says
how much each additional unit costs.
Reading those two numbers together is a
first step in judging whether a price is fair.

REPRESENTATION
A graph is a correspondence between algebra and geometry. Each ordered pair becomes a
point, and a collection of points can reveal a pattern that the numbers alone might hide.
In a linear relationship, the quantity we choose is usually called the independent variable and is
plotted on the horizontal axis. The quantity that responds is the dependent variable and is plotted
on the vertical axis. Time is often independent because we choose when to measure; distance, cost
or height is often dependent because it responds to time or to the amount used.
A table of values is a list of ordered pairs. To plot 
, substitute a few values of , calculate
the corresponding values of , and plot the resulting pairs. Because the rule is linear, two correctly
plotted points would determine the line, but a third point is a useful check.

question: how much does the dependent quantity change for each additional unit of the

horizontal line has gradient 0 because the vertical change is 0. A vertical line has an undefined
gradient because the horizontal change is 0 and division by zero is undefined. “No slope” is not the

MODELS
A linear model is a deliberately simple description of a relationship. Its value lies in
prediction and comparison, but its simplicity also limits what it can claim.
To build a linear model, name the variables and units, identify the fixed amount as the intercept
and the repeated amount as the gradient, then write 
. In a cost model, the intercept is the
amount paid before any use and the gradient is the marginal cost of one more unit. Comparing two
models means comparing both numbers: a lower intercept favours light users, while a lower
gradient favours heavy users.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Relationships. An equation or inequality is a
condition on a variable. Solving it means finding
every value that makes the condition true, not
merely producing a number that looks plausible.
Equivalence. Each step in a solution must
preserve the solution set. Adding, subtracting,
multiplying or dividing both sides by the same
non-zero number produces an equivalent
equation; multiplying or dividing an inequality
by a negative number calls for special care.
Systems. Two conditions at once restrict the
possible values more than either condition alone.
Geometrically, a system of two linear equations
asks where two lines meet; a system of
inequalities describes a region of possible
allocations.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Globalization and sustainability.
Exploration: how communities allocate
limited land, water, energy and labour
among competing uses, and how
mathematical constraints make the trade-
offs visible.
Sustainability is not only an environmental
idea; it is a problem of allocation. A garden,
a clinic or a workshop has finite resources.
Writing the limits as inequalities turns a
debate about priorities into a set of feasible
plans that can be compared, tested and
questioned.

A single equation with two variables has infinitely many solutions. Two equations

solve one equation for one variable, substitute that expression into the other equation, and solve
the resulting one-variable equation.

KEY IDEAS
Equivalent equations have the same solution
set; each operation must be applied to both
sides.
Clearing brackets and fractions before
isolating the variable reduces errors.
An identity has infinitely many solutions; a
contradiction has none.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a
negative number reverses its direction.
A solution set can be shown on a number
line or written in interval notation.
Simultaneous equations can be solved
graphically, by substitution or by
elimination.
Parallel lines give no solution; coincident
lines give infinitely many.
A system of inequalities has a feasible
region; a linear objective is optimised at a
vertex, subject to integer constraints.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Form. A shape's form is fixed by its sides, angles
and proportions. Transformations show what is
preserved when a figure moves; congruence
criteria state which measurements fix a triangle
completely.
Space. Position and orientation in the plane.
Coordinates make transformations calculable,
and symmetry describes an object that maps
onto itself.
Justification. Congruence criteria turn measured
facts into deductions; a proof records each step
so that another person can check it.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Personal and cultural expression.
Exploration: how designers and artisans use
transformations, symmetry and tessellation
to build pattern, and how mathematical
structure limits what repeated tiles can
make.
A woven band, a tiled courtyard and a
printed logo can all be described by the
same three moves: slide, flip, turn.
Mathematics does not explain why a pattern
moves us, but it explains which patterns
continue without gaps and how a repetition
can be specified precisely enough to
reproduce.

CRITERION B · II
CRITERION D · II
PATTERNS
A shape has symmetry when a transformation maps it onto itself. Symmetry is
congruence applied to a single object, and it explains why a pattern can repeat across a
surface without gaps or overlaps.
For a regular polygon with  sides, the two symmetry numbers agree: there are  lines of symmetry
and rotational symmetry of order . For other shapes they can differ. A non-square rectangle has
two lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 2; a parallelogram that is not a rectangle
has no lines of symmetry but still has rotational symmetry of order 2; an isosceles triangle has one
line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Form. A solid is defined by its faces, edges and
vertices. A net, a set of views or a cross-section is
another representation of the same form, chosen
to make a measurement visible.
Measurement. Surface area measures the
boundary in square units; volume measures
enclosed space in cubic units. Both depend on
length, but differently, and must be reported in
matching units.
Models and change. A formula models an ideal
solid; real cans have seams, rims and varied wall
thickness. Scaling changes area and volume at
different rates, so large containers use less
material per litre.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Globalization and sustainability.
Exploration: packaging and material use —
how the shape of a container affects the
material consumed, the energy needed to
transport it, and the waste left behind.
A drink can is a compromise. A taller,
thinner can uses less metal for the same
volume, but it may be less stable, harder to
hold and more expensive to ship.
Mathematical optimisation does not make
the decision; it makes the trade-offs visible
and quantifiable.

FORM
A solid is a three-dimensional region, but its surface can be described by counting and
naming its parts. Those counts are not bookkeeping: for a whole family of solids they obey
a fixed relationship, and that relationship is a first example of a structural theorem.

Figure 8.1 Five standard solids. The cuboid and pyramid are polyhedra; the cylinder, cone and sphere have curved surfaces.
The names of a prism and a pyramid come from their bases. A triangular prism has triangular
bases; a pentagonal pyramid has a pentagonal base. The orientation of the solid does not change its
name: a triangular prism standing on a rectangular face is still a triangular prism, and its
triangular faces are still the bases used in the volume formula.

D E F I N I T I O N S
A polyhedron is a closed solid whose faces are polygons. A face is a flat polygonal surface, an
edge is a segment where two faces meet, and a vertex is a point where edges meet. A prism
has two congruent parallel bases joined by rectangular faces; a pyramid has one polygonal
base and triangular faces meeting at an apex. Cylinders, cones and spheres have curved
surfaces, so they are not polyhedra. A net is a flat arrangement of faces that folds into a solid.
A plan is the view from directly above; an elevation is a view from the front or the side,
looking horizontally.

Figure 9.1 Each point is one student: study time and score measured together. The points rise from left to right, so the association is

Label the axes with the quantity and its unit, and choose scales that use the available space without
distorting the pattern. The explanatory variable is usually placed on the horizontal axis because we
are asking how the response depends on it. When neither variable is clearly prior, either axis may
be used, but the choice must be stated and kept consistent when comparing plots.
Describe a scatter plot in four moves: direction (positive, negative or none), form (linear or
curved), strength (how closely the points follow the form) and unusual features (outliers, clusters
or gaps). “Positive, linear and strong, with one high outlier” is a complete description; “it goes up” is
not.
9.1
D E F I N I T I O N S
Bivariate data consists of two measurements made on the same individual, object or
occasion. The explanatory variable is the one we use to explain or predict; the response
variable is the one we measure as an outcome. A scatter plot displays each pair as a point,
with the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis. An association is a pattern in which the
response tends to change as the explanatory variable changes. An outlier is a point that does
not fit the overall pattern. A cluster is a separated group of points.

D E F I N I T I O N S
Causation means that a change in one variable produces a change in the other. A
confounding variable is a third variable that influences both the explanatory and response
variables, creating an association that is not due to a direct causal link. Reverse causation
occurs when the response variable actually influences the explanatory variable. An
observational study records variables without intervening; a controlled experiment
deliberately changes the explanatory variable and compares outcomes under otherwise
similar conditions.

A strong correlation between X and Y does not prove X causes Y.
A third variable can drive both. Controlled experiments or additional evidence are needed for causal claims.
Figure 9.5 Ice-cream sales and swimming incidents rise together, but buying ice cream does not cause swimming incidents. Hot
weather is a common cause of both. The correlation is real; the causal direction is not.
The classic alternative explanations are worth checking systematically. Is there a common cause,
such as temperature, income or age? Could the direction be reversed, with the response
influencing the explanatory variable? Could the pattern arise from selection, because the people in
the data chose themselves or were chosen in a non-random way? Could it be a coincidence,
especially in a small sample or when many possible pairs were examined? Could the variables be
measuring the same underlying quantity, such as height and arm span?

PROBLEM
A study finds that children who own more books score higher on a reading test. A newspaper
concludes that buying books raises reading scores. Identify a plausible confounding variable,
an alternative explanation involving selection, and a way to test the claim more fairly.
ANSWER Income and parental education confound the association; selection is also plausible;
random allocation or a controlled longitudinal design would test the claim.
A plausible confounder is family income or parental education. Families with more books
may also have more resources, more time for reading and more educated parents, all of
which could raise scores independently of the books.
1
Selection: families that buy many books may already value reading; the children may differ
from those with few books before any book is bought.
2
A fairer test would randomly allocate books to some families and not others, then compare
reading scores after a fixed period, keeping other support similar.
3
If a controlled trial is impossible, a longitudinal study could track children before and after
books arrive, controlling for income and parental education. The conclusion would still be
tentative.

Explanatory variable: whether music is played (two conditions: music or no music).
Response variable: a measure of concentration, such as the number of correctly completed

Control: a no-music condition using the same task, time and classroom conditions.

condition.
4
Repeat: a single session cannot rule out coincidence. Repeat across several sessions and
compare average performance, reporting variability as well as the mean.

Logic. Probability reasons from a clearly defined

Most real questions combine events: rain and a delayed bus, a red counter and then
another red, a student who studies both languages. A representation that makes the
overlap visible is the safest way to count.

overlap first, then fill in the “only” regions, and check that all the counts add to the total.

JUSTIFICATION
A probability describes a model. A survey describes people. The bridge between them is
the sample: a small group chosen so that what is true of the group is likely to be roughly
true of the whole.

Figure 10.6 A biased sample over-represents one group, while a random sample gives every group a chance. Sample size alone
cannot repair a method that systematically misses part of the population.
Random selection is the strongest defence against bias, but it is not the only decision. A sample also
needs a complete frame: if the list omits students who are absent, or people without a phone, the
“random” draw is random only from the part that could be reached. Three common methods are:
Convenience samples — asking the first 
 people in the queue — and voluntary-response samples —
inviting anyone to vote online — are not random. They are cheap, but they systematically favour
people who are easy to reach or strongly motivated, and no increase in size removes that direction
of error.
10.4
D E F I N I T I O N S
The population is the whole group about which we want information. A sample is the part
we actually observe, and the sample size is the number of individuals in it. A census
measures every member of the population. A random sample gives every member a known,
non-zero chance of being chosen. The sampling frame is the list from which the sample is
drawn. Bias is a systematic tendency for a sample or measurement to differ from the
population in a particular direction. A representative sample has roughly the same
composition as the population on the characteristics that matter. A stratified sample selects
from each subgroup in proportion to its size.
Simple random sample. Number the frame and use a random-number generator to choose
individuals. Every member has the same chance.
Systematic sample. Choose every th name on the frame after a random start. Convenient when the
list is long, provided the list has no repeating pattern that matches .

Stratified sample. Divide the population into groups such as year levels or regions, then sample
within each group in proportion to its size. This guarantees representation of every group.

entries below show the reasoning behind each result, so a difference
between your work and mine becomes a precise question rather than
a guess about what went wrong.
HOW EACH ENTRY IS ARRANGED
Exercise numbers match the chapter. Part
letters follow the number, for example 3c.
Working is shown wherever it helps you locate
a disagreement; routine arithmetic is
compressed to a single line. Units and
rounding are stated with each result.
Some questions invite more than one valid
route. The key gives one efficient method and,
where useful, a note beginning Alternatively. A
different correct method is not an error.
Validity, accuracy and a conclusion that
answers the question are what count.
Each chapter closes with a mixed practice set
and a criterion task. Mixed-practice answers
are labelled F (fluency), R (reasoning), A
(application) and E (extension) to match the
question tags. A marking guide follows the
criterion task in most chapters.
INVESTIGATIONS AND CRITERION TASKS
Open tasks receive sample responses, not a
single script: representative data, a conjecture,
a verification and a limitation. Your data may
differ. Use the sample to judge the
completeness of your table, the quality of your
generalisation and the care of your conclusion.
Academic honesty. These solutions support your
attempt; they do not replace it. If you use a sample
response, rewrite the reasoning in your own words
and explain the choice of method. That is the
evidence a teacher can assess.

net — a flat pattern that folds to make
a solid.
non-response — failure of selected
individuals to reply to a survey, a
common source of bias.
order of magnitude — the nearest
power of ten to a quantity.
outcome — one possible result of a
probability experiment.
outlier — a value that lies far from the
general pattern of the data.
percentage point — a unit for the
difference between two percentages.
polyhedron — a solid whose faces are
flat polygons.
population — the whole group about
which information is wanted.
positive predictive value — the
proportion of positive results that are
true positives.
precision — how close repeated
measurements are to each other.
prevalence — the proportion of a
population that has a condition at a
given time.
prism — a solid with a constant cross-
section along its length.
probability — a number between 0
and 1 measuring how likely an event
is.
proof — a chain of reasoning that
establishes a statement beyond doubt
from agreed starting points.
proof by contradiction — a proof
that assumes the opposite of the claim
and shows it leads to an impossibility.
range (function) — the set of values
that a function produces as outputs.
range (statistics) — the largest value
in a data set minus the smallest.
random sample — a sample in which
every member of the population has a
known, non-zero chance of selection.
rational number — a number that
can be written as a fraction of two
integers.
reflection — a transformation that
flips a shape across a line without
changing lengths or angles.
regression to the mean — the
tendency of extreme measurements
to be followed by less extreme ones.
relative frequency — the number of
times an outcome occurred divided
by the number of trials.
relative risk — one risk divided by
another, used to compare them as a
ratio.
representative — describing a
sample with roughly the same
composition as the population.
residual — the observed value minus
the value predicted by a model.
response variable — the variable
plotted on the vertical axis, measured
in response to the other.
risk — the probability of an unwanted
outcome.
rotation — a transformation that
turns a shape about a fixed point by a
given angle.
rotational symmetry — a shape has
rotational symmetry if some rotation
maps it onto itself.
sample — the part of a population
that is actually observed.
sample space — the set of all possible
outcomes of a probability
experiment.
sampling frame — the list from
which a sample is drawn.
sampling variation — the differences
between estimates from different
random samples of the same
population.
scatter plot — a graph plotting paired
bivariate data as points.
scientific notation — a number
written as 
 with 
.
self-selection — bias caused by
individuals choosing whether to take
part.
sensitivity — the proportion of
people with a condition that a test
correctly identifies.
significant figures — the digits of a
number that carry meaning about its
precision.
similar — having the same shape but
not necessarily the same size.
simulation — a model that imitates a
probability experiment, often using
random digits.
simultaneous equations — two or
more equations that must be satisfied
at the same time.
solid — a three-dimensional shape
with faces, edges and vertices.
specificity — the proportion of people
without a condition that a test
correctly clears.
sphere — the set of points at a fixed
distance from a centre; its volume is
.
standard form — another name for
scientific notation, 
.
stratified sample — a sample that
selects from each subgroup in
proportion to its size.
subset — a set whose elements all
belong to a larger set.
surd — an expression containing a
root of a number that is not a perfect
power, such as 
.
surface area — the total area of all the
faces of a solid.
systematic sample — a sample
formed by taking every th member
of a frame after a random start.
tangent — the trigonometric ratio
opposite divided by adjacent; also a
line touching a curve at one point.
tessellation — a tiling of the plane by
shapes with no gaps or overlaps.
theorem — a mathematical statement
that has been proved.
transformation — a change in the
position, size or orientation of a
shape.
translation — a transformation that
slides every point the same distance
in the same direction.
tree diagram — a diagram showing
the stages of a multi-stage experiment
and their probabilities.
trial — one repetition of a probability
experiment.
two-way table — a table recording
counts for two categorical variables at
once.
union —

 or both.
universal set — the set  containing
every outcome or element under
discussion, shown as a rectangle.
validity — the extent to which a
method measures what it claims to
measure.
Venn diagram — a diagram using
overlapping regions to show sets and
their relationships.
vertex — a corner of a solid or
polygon where edges meet.
volume — the space occupied by a
solid, measured in cubic units.
voluntary-response sample — a
sample made of people who choose to
reply; strongly self-selected.
with replacement — describing a
draw in which the item is returned
before the next draw, keeping
probabilities constant.
without replacement — describing a
draw in which the item is not
returned, changing later
probabilities.
